chunks: When to use and skip test points. The question: When should/shouldn't you use them?
A test point earns its place only if what it tells you is worth what it costs. You use one where a fault would show up and you cannot see it any other way.
You skip or adapt it where it would harm the signal, create a safety problem, or duplicate access you already have. The decision is made net by net.
Think of putting inspection hatches in a building. You want one near the main water valve and the electrical panel, where problems start and where plumbers need access.
You would not cut a hatch where a window already shows the pipe, or in a spot where the hatch would weaken the wall.
A test point works like that: it gives a view, but it also takes space and may disturb the signal.
A per-net decision flow. Most nets end at "standard pad"; the interesting engineering is in the special-case branch.
Net: all the copper that forms one electrical connection. Power rail: a net that carries a supply voltage.
Boundary scan: using chips' own pin controls to check connections you cannot probe. Stub: a short spur of copper from the signal to the pad.
Reflection: part of a fast signal bouncing back because of a bump in the line.
A test pad adds about 0. 5 picofarads with its stub.
On a slow power rail this does nothing, so power rails, ground, resets, clocks, programming lines and key analog points all get test points.
On a fast signal line (a standard 50 ohms one) whose edge, the time to switch from low to high, is 100 picoseconds, a tenth of a nanosecond, the same 0.
5 picofarads reflects about 12. 5 % of the signal. So fast nets get a special in-line pad, a shielded coaxial connector, or no pad at all. That is the whole idea.
"I add test points where the information is worth the cost: rails, ground, resets, power-good, programming lines, slow buses and key analog nodes.
I skip or modify them on high-speed, RF, high-impedance and oscillator nets, where the pad adds capacitance and a stub, and on nets I can already see through a connector, boundary scan or self-test.
High-voltage nets need guarded points. I decide per net by value, user, alternatives and cost."
